# Michael Wallman for Berkeley City Council, District 8
Berkeley City Council · District 8
Change is on the way.
As a lifelong Berkeley resident, I can say decisively that our city needs urgent change, grounded in common sense policy and leadership that truly delivers results.
DonateOrder Yard Signs & Swag
Fred Feller endorses Michael
Wallman 1st, Mendonca 2nd.
## Endorsed by
- Flip the Berkeley City Council
- Save Berkeley Shops Action Fund
A District 8 candidate endorses Michael
## Fred Feller left the race.
He's backing Wallman.
“My supporters and I whole-heartedly endorse Michael Wallman for District 8. We suggest ranked-choice voting for Michael Wallman as #1 and Mari Mendonca as #2.”
Fred FellerAttorney · Former District 8 candidate
See how to mark your ballot
Read Fred's statement
Still on your ballot
The ballot was finalized in August, so Fred M. Feller is still printed in District 8. Fred asks you to rank Wallman 1st and Mendonca 2nd instead.
About Fred
- Fifty years as a lawyer for Bay Area tenants and property owners
- Served on Berkeley's Police Review Commission and Housing Advisory Commission
- Vice President of the board of Bay Area Legal Aid
- Past President of the Berkeley Albany Bar Association
- Lives in the Elmwood, in the heart of District 8
## About Me
Berkeley is central to my story.
My parents — a Lebanese mother and Finnish father — met as graduate students at the International House. Born in Oakland, they brought me home as a newborn to a small apartment on Dwight Way. Soon after, we moved near Lawrence Hall, where my two sisters arrived. My mother worked as a librarian for the City of Berkeley and for the Berkeley public schools, and my father was a scientist and lecturer at Cal. Lacking any extended family in the U.S., our immediate neighbors and local community became my family.
I attended all of Berkeley's public schools, community college, and UC Berkeley, earning a degree in Electrical Engineering, Computer Science, and Material Science. While in college, I worked as a lab tech in downtown Berkeley and in the restaurant industry. Since graduating, I have helped found Berkeley-based startups and worked in big tech.
Today, my wife — a first-generation Mexican-American from East Oakland — and I are raising our two children on Panoramic Hill. We care for my mother-in-law in our home, while my mother and stepdad live near Monterey Market. Caring for this community is deeply personal to me.
## Why I'm Running
Berkeley needs better.
For years, we have endured long and uncoordinated road and sidewalk closures, blocks of vacant storefronts, littered streets, failing infrastructure, unbalanced budgets, and leadership that is out of touch with local realities.
Despite adding thousands of housing units, rents remain high; meanwhile, BART and AC Transit ridership, along with school district enrollment, have all declined. While our leaders promised a car-free future supported by bikes and transit, the reality is a wave of ride-share and delivery drivers, sidewalks cluttered with electric scooters, crumbling roads, and a decade of development that has failed to lower costs in any meaningful way.
To build an equitable and vibrant Berkeley, we must reject this trajectory. The city needs representatives who understand new AI technologies, who rely on verified data for decision-making, who listen to their constituents, who can create local jobs, and who speak out against injustice, wherever it may lie. If you support this vision for our future, I ask for your vote.
The SeatChallenging an incumbentMark Humbert
The FocusHousing, traffic safety, UC Berkeley
Election DayNovember 3, 2026
## Top of Mind
What I'm focused on for District 8
Tap any priority to read more.
1
### Housing For All
Berkeley's housing debate has become all-or-nothing. We need genuinely affordable, family-sized homes — not just dormitory-style blocks — and a streamlined permitting process that makes it easier to build for homeowners.
Our community requires residential spaces designed for long-term family vitality, rather than transient occupancy. This necessitates sensible three- to four-story scale developments within residential neighborhoods situated away from downtown and major transit corridors, such as specific stretches of San Pablo Avenue.
While I do not claim to have every answer or a total grasp of every complex zoning regulation, the data I have examined is deeply concerning:
- Berkeley continues to fall short of its targets for both low-income and middle-income housing.
- A significant majority of new units are rentals, eroding the traditional role of property as a tool for local wealth generation.
- Development is heavily skewed toward one-bedroom and studio apartments rather than family-sized homes.
- Parking mandates have been removed, and essential spaces are frequently excluded to cut development costs.
My approach to delivering new housing relies on several core initiatives:
- 1Establish open, organized housing datasets to ensure complete policy transparency. Informed decision-making requires verified metrics covering constructed, active, and proposed units, categorized by bedroom count, parking, outdoor spaces, tenure type, and proximity to essential services or transit.
- 2Streamline red tape for resident-led developments across our approximately 20,000 single-family parcels, driving organic, neighborhood-scale expansion instead of relying exclusively on high-density downtown models.
- 3Conduct a thorough council retrospective to identify structural barriers causing stagnant corridor development and stalled projects (like downtown), establishing clear key performance indicators and actionable target objectives.
- 4Implement policy frameworks like Community Benefit Programs to facilitate thoughtful density while preserving neighborhood character and architectural standards.
- 5Protect historic districts and significant structures. As a resident in a contributing property within the Panoramic Hill Historic District, I remain committed to expanding historic designations that safeguard the architectural fabric defining our city.
- 6Cultivate closer partnerships with commercial stakeholders and advocate for mixed-use, mixed-income builders to prevent isolating neighborhoods by income tiers.
My perspective is straightforward: unless the city makes direct investments in truly affordable housing, partners effectively with developers, and helps homeowners scale their own properties, Berkeley will be defined by massive, dormitory-style blocks that fail our community.
2
### Claremont Slow Down
Claremont Avenue outside an elementary school needs a real signal and real traffic safety — not temporary plastic posts.
After an uplands neighborhood association meeting, a resident voiced frustration over dangerous traffic district-wide. Walking my children across Claremont Avenue to John Muir Elementary, I have long wondered why an active school zone lacks a proper signal.
Watching the Star Market intersection next morning confirmed these concerns. Commuters speed down Claremont on mobile devices while cyclists struggle to navigate.
To address these challenges effectively, I propose the following short-term and long-term strategic initiatives:
- 1Sustained Speed Enforcement: Partner directly with the Berkeley Police Department to institute persistent, continuous traffic control throughout the Claremont corridor rather than relying on brief, sporadic operations.
- 2Cyclist Priority Safeguards: Install explicit street signage and high-visibility pavement markings to formally designate the right lane as a dedicated right-of-way for cyclists.
- 3Timely Infrastructure Repairs: Although major repaving and restriping initiatives remain tied to the forthcoming underground bypass project, deteriorating roadway conditions may demand immediate attention regardless of timeline delays.
- 4Utility Undergrounding Coordination: Engage promptly with PG&E and EBMUD to evaluate placing power and communications lines subterranean, guaranteeing that necessary conduit installation proceeds alongside the bypass construction.
- 5Illumination Upgrades: Modernize and upgrade street lighting across Claremont Avenue and surrounding Uplands residential areas.
- 6Data-Driven Traffic Analysis: Launch a comprehensive metric collection framework analyzing pedestrian activity, vehicle counts, and parking usage—highlighted by an Origin-Destination study—while evaluating adjacent arterial routes to assess neighborhood impacts from potential capacity reductions on Claremont.
#### Sources
- Underground Bypass – Zone No. 12 (Claremont Avenue) — Alameda County Public Works Agency
3
### Cal as a Good Neighbor
No district feels Cal's decisions more than District 8 — we need a representative who works with the university and defends the neighborhood.
Due to its close proximity to Cal, District 8 is particularly impacted by the university's decisions. Cal is the 800-pound gorilla in the room—a complex maze of bureaucracy and regulations, much like the city itself. For many residents, it remains a love-hate relationship.
- Our housing crisis in Berkeley was driven in part by increasing student admissions without a corresponding, joint housing plan created alongside the city.
- The University continues to push development deep into Strawberry Canyon, constructing stadiums illuminated for modern broadcast athletics. No public transit, nor meaningful pedestrian infrastructure exist in these locations.
- Financing the stadium project has created a severe debt burden.
- The University continues to concentrate parking on Bancroft Way, where its new structure, opened in September 2026, funnels roughly 600 cars onto a street already narrowed by Class 4 bike corridors and dedicated bus lanes—a combination that predictably creates severe traffic bottlenecks for District 8.
- Under the UC Berkeley–City of Berkeley Settlement Agreement, the University pays the City about $4.75 million this year ($4.1 million in 2021, rising 3% annually) — roughly one-seventh of the more than $32 million the University of Michigan provided Ann Arbor in fiscal year 2025.
We need a representative who works closely with the University while steadfastly defending the best interests of Berkeley and, above all, District 8 residents.
#### Sources
- UC Berkeley–City of Berkeley Settlement Agreement, signed July 27, 2021 (PDF)
- “UC Berkeley breaks ground on $62.6M replacement for Bancroft Parking Structure” — The Daily Californian, June 27, 2025
- Bancroft Parking Structure Replacement — UC Berkeley Capital Strategies
- “U-M contributes over $32M to Ann Arbor, local communities” — The University Record, March 30, 2026
### Also on the agenda
4
### Small Business Support
Our empty storefronts are a policy failure. Protect the neighborhood commercial districts that keep Berkeley livable.
Small businesses serve as the cornerstone of a thriving local community, going far beyond their role as economic drivers. Operating on thin profit margins makes these local shops uniquely vulnerable to operational conditions—including parking access, foot traffic, neighborhood cleanliness, and natural light.
The shortcomings of our current policy approach are glaringly evident. A stroll through Downtown Berkeley along Center Street reveals a heartbreaking wave of storefront vacancies. This problem spreads far beyond downtown: both historic structures and modern commercial spaces along University and San Pablo Avenues reflect the exact same concerning decline.
Although vibrant commercial pockets persist in areas like Elmwood, 4th Street, Hopkins, and the Alcatraz-Adeline intersection, these critical business clusters face ongoing threats.
We must safeguard these essential neighborhood hubs from the broad and targeted upzoning measures typical of major transit corridors. Sustainable growth in these sensitive zones demands closer collaboration with commercial stakeholders, prioritizing owner-occupied units and requiring construction methods that minimize disruption to pedestrian flow.
By enacting these targeted safeguards, Berkeley can foster commercial districts that are both economically resilient and deeply inclusive.
To fill lingering commercial vacancies, we need streamlined programs for faster, lower-cost small business onboarding, such as flexible pop-ups and short-term leases without major upfront or long-term commitments. Sharing foot and vehicle traffic data will also help business owners choose optimal locations to serve the community.
5
### Wildfire Safety in the Hills
Real evacuation plans and safety standards for District 8's wildland edge — before the next fire.
District 8's wildland edge is exposed. Build real evacuation plans and resident safety standards with the fire department and the university — before the next fire, not after it.
6
### Privacy, Cameras, and Smart Policing
Public safety is a civic duty — not an excuse for surveillance networks that outlive their promises and put our privacy at risk.
Residents should not have to deploy private surveillance systems because of crime; public safety remains a fundamental civic duty. While no one argues against alerts for stolen cars or violent fugitives, that is not what this technology is about. We are witnessing the creeping importation of authoritarian monitoring models — reminiscent of how governments like China use facial recognition to track citizens and suppress dissent — right into our own backyards.
Although proponents claim current cameras are restricted to license plates and basic vehicle attributes, hardware outlives software policies. As AI models rapidly evolve, these systems will easily cross the line into identifying individuals, tracking anyone in the city at any time, and morphing into automated data brokers that harvest our daily movements. Most concerning is that neither local police departments nor municipal governments possess the cybersecurity expertise required to defend against a future where sophisticated AI agents and foreign state actors can effortlessly breach networked municipal databases.
If any cameras are used at all, they should be strictly closed-circuit and limited solely to anonymous data like traffic counts and speed, completely devoid of vehicle or user identifications. Ultimately, the speculative benefits of these surveillance networks do not outweigh the profound dangers to our civil liberties and digital security. Rather than investing heavily in fragile, invasive technology, I recommend that the council instead direct those resources toward hiring additional police officers.

## Rank Wallman 1st.
Rank Mendonca 2nd.
District 8 uses ranked-choice voting. On your ballot, fill in the 1st-column oval next to Michael Wallman and the 2nd-column oval next to Mari Mendonca — and leave the rest blank.
Why Mari Mendonca
“I'm supporting Mari because of her unrelenting commitment and dedication to Berkeley and its people.”
— Michael Wallman
Your second choice never hurts your first: it only counts if your first choice is eliminated. Election Day is Tuesday, November 3.

Moonshots
Big ideas for all of Berkeley
These reach beyond District 8. They're long shots that would take real partnership to pull off — and they'd make the whole city better.
### Universal After School Care
Fund onsite after school care at every BUSD elementary school, so every family has a safe, enriching place for their kids until the workday ends — no waitlists, no scramble across town.
### Reintroduce Trade Programs at BHS
Bring hands-on career and technical education back to Berkeley High — shop, construction, automotive, electrical — so students can graduate straight into an apprenticeship or a good union job, not only a four-year degree.
### Reopen the University's Public Spaces
Work with UC Berkeley to give the community back spaces it has lost over the years — starting with Cal's turf fields, which could host neighborhood sports, leagues, and events when the teams aren't using them.
### Bring Back Willard Pool
Restore and staff Willard Pool so it can once again offer swim lessons, lap swimming, and low-impact exercise for Berkeley residents of every age.
### Save Alta Bates Medical Center
Sutter plans to move Alta Bates' emergency room and hospital beds to Emeryville, leaving Berkeley without a full-service hospital. Keep acute care here by putting every creative option on the table — a partnership with UC, a voter-backed healthcare district, or a new operator for the Ashby campus.
### More Parks for a Growing Berkeley
More homes, more people, more students — and our parks have to grow with them. Put parks in the infrastructure equation alongside roads and sewers: plan new open space with every wave of housing, and turn underused lots and street space into pocket parks and playgrounds.

## Frequently Asked
Quick answers about the race
Who is Michael Wallman?+
Michael Wallman is a lifelong Berkeley resident and engineer running for Berkeley City Council, District 8, in the November 3, 2026 election.
What district is Michael Wallman running for?+
Berkeley City Council, District 8.
When is the election?+
Election Day is November 3, 2026.
Who is Michael Wallman running against?+
Michael Wallman is challenging incumbent District 8 Councilmember Mark Humbert.
What are Michael Wallman's top priorities?+
Small business, housing that stays affordable, and holding UC Berkeley accountable as a neighbor — plus protecting tenants from displacement, wildfire safety in the hills, and smarter, privacy-respecting policing.
How can I donate to Michael Wallman's campaign?+
Online via ActBlue or by check at wallmandistrict8.com/donate. Berkeley residents giving $10–$60 can have their contribution matched 6-to-1 through the city's Fair Elections program.
How can I volunteer for the campaign?+
Sign up at wallmandistrict8.com/join.
How do I contact the campaign?+
Email info@wallmandistrict8.com or use the contact form at wallmandistrict8.com/contact.
